- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.7) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.3) or oscillating, model often underestimates or lags; increase forecast to catch upward momentum.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >+5% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots; cap forecast at 1–2% below peak or adjust downward 1–2 days.
- If sentiment flips from negative to positive mid-horizon, model often fails to adjust; re-estimate from sentiment shift point, not from historical mean.
- Mean reversion bias: if model holds steady near recent 5-day average, true price often drifts 1–3% away; adjust forecast toward 3–5 day moving average if sentiment is neutral.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overweights early sentiment; weight later sentiment (last 7–10 days) more heavily for mid-to-late forecast correction.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “0.00” or “0.50” entries, model tends to underreact; add 0.5–1.0 to forecast if sentiment is weak but price is rising.
- Overshoots after sentiment spikes are common; apply “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0% per day after sentiment peak.
